sections.title: Earth's connected spheres
sections.text:
The environment includes interacting physical, chemical and biological conditions. The atmosphere is the gaseous envelope; the hydrosphere comprises Earth's water; the lithosphere is the rigid outer shell; the biosphere comprises living systems and their occupied regions; and the cryosphere includes frozen water. These divisions help analysis but do not create isolated systems. Rain transfers water from atmosphere to land, plants move carbon between air and biomass, and weathering transfers rock-derived materials into rivers.

Feedback occurs when a change influences the process that produced it. Loss of bright snow exposes darker ground, increasing absorbed sunlight and potentially causing further warming: a positive feedback. A negative feedback counteracts the original change. Positive and negative describe direction of response, not whether a process is desirable.

sections.title: Atmospheric composition and layers
sections.text:
Dry air near the surface is approximately 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen by volume, with argon, carbon dioxide and other gases forming most of the remainder. Water vapour is variable and strongly influences weather and energy transfer. Trace concentration does not imply negligible importance: ozone and greenhouse gases have effects disproportionate to their small abundance.

The troposphere contains most familiar weather and is heated strongly through exchanges with the surface. Its temperature generally decreases with altitude, though inversions occur. The stratosphere contains much of the protective ozone layer and generally warms with height because of ultraviolet absorption. Temperature generally decreases through the mesosphere, then rises strongly in the thermosphere. The outer exosphere grades into space. Boundaries change with latitude, season and solar activity.

The ionosphere is defined by ionization, not simply one exclusive temperature layer. It overlaps parts of the upper atmosphere and influences radio propagation. Auroras involve energetic charged particles exciting atmospheric constituents within Earth's magnetic environment. High thermospheric kinetic temperatures do not mean a person would experience the same heat transfer as in dense hot air: particle density is very low.

sections.title: Water compartments and the water cycle
sections.text:
Oceans contain most Earth's water. Freshwater is distributed among ice, groundwater, lakes, rivers, soil moisture and the atmosphere. The amount stored in a compartment and the rate at which water moves through it are different quantities. Groundwater in a deep aquifer may renew slowly even where annual rainfall seems substantial.

Solar energy supports evaporation from water and land and transpiration from plants. Water vapour is transported, condenses into cloud particles and returns through precipitation. Water then runs over the surface, enters soil by infiltration or moves deeper through percolation. Groundwater flows through pores and fractures and may discharge into springs, streams or the sea.

```text
Surface water / soil / plants → evaporation and transpiration → atmosphere
→ condensation → precipitation → runoff or infiltration
→ rivers / groundwater / storage → further exchange and evaporation
```

A watershed drains toward a common outlet. An aquifer stores and transmits usable groundwater through permeable materials; an aquitard transmits much less readily. The water table marks the upper surface of an unconfined saturated zone. Pumping faster than replenishment can lower groundwater levels, increase pumping costs and contribute to land subsidence in susceptible materials. The water cycle conserves matter globally while allowing serious local shortages and contamination.

sections.title: Minerals, rocks and the rock cycle
sections.text:
A mineral is a naturally occurring solid with a characteristic composition range and ordered internal structure. A rock is an aggregate of minerals or other geological material. Identification uses properties such as hardness, cleavage, density and streak; colour alone is often unreliable.

Igneous rocks form when molten material cools. Slow cooling underground commonly permits larger crystals, while rapid surface cooling commonly produces fine-grained or glassy textures. Sedimentary rocks form through deposition and lithification or chemical and biological accumulation. Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks change under pressure, temperature or fluids without complete melting.

| Rock type | Formation process | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Igneous | Cooling of magma or lava | Granite, basalt |
| Sedimentary | Deposition, cementation or chemical accumulation | Sandstone, shale, limestone |
| Metamorphic | Solid-state transformation | Marble, slate, gneiss |

Weathering breaks or alters rock in place; erosion transports material. Physical weathering fragments rock, while chemical weathering changes minerals through reactions such as dissolution or hydrolysis. Soil develops through weathering, biological activity and redistribution of material. A soil profile can contain distinct horizons, but horizon development varies with climate, organisms, topography, parent material and time.

The rock cycle connects melting, crystallization, weathering, transport, deposition, burial and metamorphism. It is a network of possible pathways rather than one mandatory circular journey for every rock.

sections.title: Plate tectonics and Earth's interior
sections.text:
Earth has a crust, mantle and core. The core includes a liquid outer region and a solid inner region. The lithosphere comprises crust and the uppermost rigid mantle and is divided into moving plates. Beneath it, the asthenosphere can deform over geological time. The mantle is predominantly solid rock capable of slow flow, not a universal ocean of liquid magma.

Divergent boundaries separate plates and can create new oceanic lithosphere. Convergent boundaries bring plates together, producing subduction or continental collision. Transform boundaries accommodate lateral movement. Oceanic lithosphere generally cools and becomes denser with age, contributing to subduction where conditions permit. Slab pull, ridge-related forces and mantle flow interact in plate motion.

Pakistan's tectonic setting includes continental collision in the north and subduction-related processes toward the Makran margin. This helps explain strong geographic variation in earthquake and mountain-building processes. Plate tectonics connects long-term landscape development with the hazards examined in Chapter 5.

sections.title: Ecosystems, biomes and food webs
sections.text:
An ecosystem includes organisms and their physical environment interacting through energy flow and material cycling. A population comprises members of a species in an area; a community includes interacting populations. Habitat is where an organism lives, while niche includes its ecological relationships and resource use.

Producers build organic compounds using light or chemical energy. Consumers obtain organic material from other organisms. Decomposers process dead material and wastes, returning nutrients to circulation. Food chains show simple pathways, while food webs describe multiple connections. Energy is transferred inefficiently between trophic levels and ultimately dissipates as heat; nutrients cycle but energy does not circulate indefinitely in the same usable form. A fixed “ten percent” transfer is a teaching approximation, not an exact constant for every ecosystem.

Biomes are broad ecological regions influenced strongly by climate and vegetation. Tropical forests, temperate forests, grasslands, deserts and tundra differ in temperature, water availability and biological adaptations. Aquatic ecosystems include freshwater, marine and transitional environments such as estuaries. Within Pakistan, mountains, arid landscapes, agricultural plains, wetlands and coastal mangroves support different ecological conditions.

sections.title: Biogeochemical cycles
sections.text:
The carbon cycle connects photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, oceans, sediments and geological processes. Fossil-fuel combustion transfers long-stored carbon into active atmospheric circulation. Ocean uptake involves chemical equilibria, so added carbon dioxide can alter seawater acidity as well as carbon storage.

Nitrogen gas is abundant but unavailable directly to most organisms. Biological fixation converts it into reactive forms. Assimilation incorporates nitrogen into biomass, ammonification returns organic nitrogen toward ammonium, nitrification oxidizes ammonium toward nitrate, and denitrification can return nitrate-derived nitrogen to gaseous forms. These stages involve different organisms and conditions.

Phosphorus cycles mainly through rocks, soil, water and organisms and lacks a large rapidly cycling atmospheric gas reservoir analogous to nitrogen gas. Weathering releases phosphate, organisms assimilate it and sediments can store it. These cycles explain why excessive fertilizer or sewage nutrients can stimulate aquatic growth, as developed in Chapter 17.

questions.prompt: Why is the phosphorus cycle different from the nitrogen cycle at the global scale?

options.A: Phosphorus does not occur in living cells
options.C: Phosphorus exists only as an atmospheric gas
options.D: Phosphorus lacks a comparably large rapidly cycling atmospheric gaseous reservoir

questions.explanation: Phosphorus cycling involves rocks, sediments, soils and water rather than a major gaseous reservoir analogous to atmospheric N₂.

questions.prompt: Why does temperature generally increase with altitude through much of the stratosphere?

options.A: Oxygen is absent from the stratosphere
options.B: Ozone-related absorption of solar ultraviolet radiation contributes to heating
options.D: Every layer is warmed only by geothermal heat

questions.explanation: Stratospheric ozone absorbs significant ultraviolet radiation, producing a characteristic vertical temperature structure.

questions.prompt: Auroras occur chiefly through interactions involving:

options.C: Energetic charged particles and Earth's upper atmosphere/magnetic environment

questions.explanation: Energetic particles excite atmospheric constituents; their subsequent emissions produce auroral light.

questions.prompt: A catchment is deforested and much rainfall runs rapidly off the surface. What groundwater consequence is plausible?

options.A: Reduced infiltration and recharge under some conditions
options.B: Complete elimination of the water cycle
options.C: Instant replacement of groundwater by magma

questions.explanation: Land cover and soil disturbance can change infiltration and groundwater recharge. Actual effects depend on soil, geology and rainfall.

questions.prompt: In many freshwater ecosystems, why is phosphorus management particularly important?

options.B: Phosphorus is always a radioactive gas
options.D: Phosphorus supply can limit primary production, so excess inputs may stimulate blooms

questions.explanation: Phosphorus is an important limiting nutrient in many freshwater systems, although nitrogen and other factors can also matter.

questions.prompt: At an oceanic convergent boundary, one plate may subduct partly because:

options.A: The older, cooler oceanic lithosphere can become sufficiently dense to sink beneath another plate
options.C: Earth's rotation directly melts every plate
options.D: Ocean water pulls the Moon into the crust

questions.explanation: Oceanic lithosphere changes density with cooling and aging; buoyancy and plate forces help determine subduction dynamics.
